title: Context boundary exploration — notes & small experiments
content:
Quick orientation
-- why I care: production apps keep hitting weird behaviour when prompt length crosses certain thresholds (abrupt drop in slot-filling accuracy, hallucination spikes). Need better intuition for: where is the model "boundary" vs our infra (KV cache, batching, truncation)?

Reading highlights (short + my takeaways)
1) "Chunked Retrieval + Re-rank for Long Context" (internal reading notes)
   - idea: treat retrieval hits as soft prefixes, re-rank short chunks rather than stitching huge context.
   - takeaway: re-ranking reduces noise but adds latency; tradeoff sweet spot is 2-4 chunks at 512 tokens each for our typical docs.
   - infra implication: can send 2 parallel retrieval requests and 1 re-ranker call; need per-request latency budget < 80ms for search + 120ms for re-rank to keep overall < 250ms.

2) "KV warmup dynamics" (paper X; lecture notes)
   - observation: initial tokens are expensive and influence subsequent attention distribution; models show higher perplexity until KV buffer fills with topical tokens.
   - my experiment idea: measure downstream QA accuracy vs warmup length (0, 8, 32 tokens) while fixing total token budget. Expected: small warmup (8) reduces hallucination on first answer generation.

3) "Prefix-caching vs Full-KV caching" (various docs + Slack threads)
   - prefix cache (store final layer activations for common instruction prefixes) helps latency but can mismatch when retrieval returns slightly changed phrasing.
   - heuristics: use fuzzy-match threshold on prefix hash; store multiple prefix variants with LRU; serve fallback to full KV when mismatch probability high.

Handy quotes / paraphrases
- "Metrics don't lie, but they don't tell the whole story" — meaning accuracy vs user-perceived quality diverge when latency constraints force truncation.
- "There is often an infra-induced cliff, not a model one" — i.e., our batching/pinning policies sometimes cause large effective context drops when queueing behavior changes.

Notes-to-self: quick experiments to run (priority order)
A) Controlled QA degrade curve (high value)
   - dataset: 500 short QA pairs + 100 multi-document synthesis tasks
   - experiment axes: total_context_budget (512..8192), retrieval_chunks (0,1,3), warmup_tokens (0,8,32), quantized vs fp16 model variant
   - metrics: exact match / F1, rouge-L for synth, hallucination score (binary heuristic), tail latency p95, cost/tokens
   - infra: use dedicated dev pool (dev-dedicated-2) pinned to A100-40GB; disable autoscaling; single client concurrency 8
   - success criterion: identify contiguous region where quality drops >8% but latency improves <50ms — that's where we can apply adaptive fallback.

B) KV-cache divergence test (low effort)
   - create 200 synthetic prompts where retrieval returns paraphrases of same doc. Compare: prefix-cache hit rate vs full-kv match, and check accuracy difference.
   - log: prefix_hash, fuzzy_score, answer_variance.

C) Batch shape stress test (ops)
   - vary batch sizes with same avg sequence length; monitor model kernel selection (int8 path vs fp16), GPU utilization, and per-token latency. Hypothesis: at certain batch shapes our kernel selector swaps to a slower matmul routine. Confirm.

Quick implementation notes / commands (for me)
- use bench harness: scripts/bench/context-boundary-run.py --dataset data/qas-small.json --model redwood/open-7b-v2 --budget 2048 --retrieval-chunks 3 --warmup 8 --concurrency 8 --out results/ctx-boundary/ (add --dry-run to validate)
- log format should include prefix_hash, kv_hits, kv_size_bytes, kernel_version, gpu_sm_util, p50/p95_latency_ms, cost_per_1k_tokens

Open questions + hypotheses (to log in experiments)
- Q1: Is the apparent cliff in accuracy correlated more strongly with token budget or with kernel selection change? (need to capture kernel_version at inference time)
- Q2: Do paraphrase-heavy retrievals cause more prefix-cache misses than literal-match returns? (likely yes; quantify fuzzy threshold)
- Q3: Can we design a cheap re-ranker model that runs on CPU to avoid re-rank latency? Rough idea: compressed lightweight bi-encoder + small cross-encoder fallback.

Small design sketch: adaptive context controller
- Inputs: client SLA (p95 latency target), query complexity signal (estimated from prompt length + retrieval score), recent model quality signal (rolling eval on held-out prompts)
- Outputs: routing decision: {use-full-context, chunk+rerank, reduce_retrieval, use-quantized-variant}
- Policy heuristics: if p95 latency budget tight and retrieval precision high -> chunk+re-rank; if warmup token cost high and chain-of-thought needed -> use-full-context on dedicated pool
- Implementation notes: stateless policy server (lambda) reads recent metrics from metrics-store, outputs policy; minimal state in request path to keep latency small.

Logging / instrumentation changes asked for
- add kernel_version to token-level traces
- export prefix_hash and fuzzy_score for every retrieval hit
- push per-request 'quality_score' from eval harness if available

Useful links I keep returning to
- internal: confluence/context-boundary-playbook (linked above)
- notes: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07198 (example paper on memory caching patterns)
- discussion: https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C0INFER/p1670001110000

Todo (next week)
- get Owen's help to wire kernel_version into traces (JIRA-1129 assigned)
- run small KV divergence test (target: Monday morning run)
- prototype tiny re-ranker on CPU (Mika volunteered to pair)

Random brain-dump / fragments (will sort later)
- consider hybrid caching: prefix cache for first N tokens + streaming KV for remainder. Possibly a cheaper prefix fingerprint + small Bloom filter to avoid heavy false positives.
- think about UX: if app notices hallucination spike, surface "context limit encountered" to users? risky.

End notes: this doc is intentionally messy. Goal is an executable set of small experiments and an emergent design for adaptive routing. Will move proven bits to confluence + add a one-pager once we have a crisp curve.
